title: Faith after
hookLine: some survivors lost faith, some kept it, some argued with God; all are honored

cards: Elie Wiesel told a story from the camp where he was held. A few prisoners, learned men, decided to put God on trial. They argued the case through the nights, like a court.
At the end, they reached a verdict: guilty. And then, the story goes, one of them looked up and said it was time for the evening prayer. And they prayed.
Hold both halves of that story at once: the verdict, and the prayer.

teach.b: Survivors came out of the Holocaust with faith in very different shapes. Some lost it. They had prayed, the prayers seemed to meet nothing, and they could not go back.
Some kept it. They rebuilt synagogues, said Kaddish for their parents, taught their children the blessings over bread and candles. That answer is honored too.
And some argued: they kept speaking to God, and the speaking was a fight. That third way has deep roots in the Tanakh.

When Abraham hears that Sodom will be destroyed, he argues to God's face: "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly?" The psalmist, feeling abandoned, shouts upward: "Awake, why sleepest Thou, O Lord?"
Job argues his case at length, and at the end God says that Job has spoken rightly, and his comforters have not. In this tradition, arguing with God can itself be a kind of prayer.
After the war, Jewish thinkers offered many answers, and none of them won. Some reached for an old phrase from Deuteronomy, hester panim, God hiding the face.
Some said there is no answer, and that building one would wrong the dead. Some said the only answer was to go on living as Jews, so the story would not end there. This path doesn't pick among them.
The one who stopped praying, the one who never stopped, the one who prayed through clenched teeth: each is honored, and none is ours to judge.

how: Jewish communities hold a wide range of responses to the Holocaust side by side; on Yom HaShoah, memorial services may include psalms, the memorial prayer and Kaddish, and also readings of doubt and protest.

games.q: you're one of the prisoners who has just found God guilty. evening comes. what do you do?
games.why: in the story Wiesel told, someone said it was time for the evening prayer, and they prayed.

practice: Bring up one question you carry that has no tidy answer, about suffering, about God, or about someone you lost, and hold it the way you'd hold something heavy that isn't yours to set down yet.
When your mind races toward an answer, come back to the question itself. If you pray, bring it to God just as it is, argument and all; if not, let it sit beside you in the quiet.

wordCard.voice: Faith after. What survivors did with faith after the Holocaust: some lost it, some kept it, some argued with God.
